title: Psychology & people
entries: What people really want

Most people want to feel respected, understood, and in control of their own choices. Arguments that threaten someone's status or autonomy get rejected even when they're correct. Make it easy for them to agree without losing face.
Reciprocity
People feel obligated to return favors, concessions and kindness. It's why free samples work and why giving first builds trust. It also gets exploited: unrequested 'gifts' are often a setup.
Social proof
When unsure, people copy what others are doing. Crowds, reviews and 'everyone's doing it' are powerful and often wrong. Ask whether the crowd actually knows anything you don't.
Commitment and consistency

Once people publicly commit to something, they bend over backwards to stay consistent with it. Small yeses lead to bigger ones. Useful for building habits; dangerous when it locks you into a bad position.
Scarcity
Things seem more valuable when rare or about to disappear. 'Only 2 left' and countdown timers are scarcity plays. Ask: would I want this if there were a thousand of them?
Projection
Attributing your own feelings or motives to someone else. People who constantly accuse others of lying or cheating are sometimes describing themselves.
Cognitive dissonance
The discomfort of holding two conflicting beliefs, or acting against your values. People usually resolve it by changing the belief, not the behavior: 'I smoke, but it's not that bad.'
Emotional reasoning
Treating a feeling as proof: 'I feel like a failure, so I am one.' Feelings are real information about your state, not reliable information about reality.
Attachment styles

A rough model of how people bond: secure (comfortable with closeness), anxious (fears abandonment, needs reassurance), avoidant (uncomfortable with dependence, pulls away). It's a lens, not a diagnosis, and people can become more secure.
Red flags in people

Consistent patterns matter more than single incidents: blaming everyone else, rules that apply to you but not them, love-bombing then withdrawal, isolating you from friends, punishing honesty, and charm that switches off when they don't need you.
Green flags in people
Keeps small promises, admits mistakes without being forced, respects 'no', is the same person in private and in public, is happy for your wins, and handles disagreement without contempt.
Gaslighting

Making someone doubt their own memory or perception ('that never happened', 'you're too sensitive') to gain control. Counter: write things down, check with trusted people, trust patterns over persuasion.
Contempt
Eye-rolling, mockery and disgust toward a partner is one of the strongest predictors of a relationship failing. Complaints about behavior are fixable; contempt for the person is corrosive.
The spotlight effect
People overestimate how much others notice and remember their mistakes, looks, and awkward moments. Everyone is mostly thinking about themselves.
Impostor syndrome
Feeling like a fraud despite evidence of competence, common in capable people who are learning fast. The fix is evidence: list what you've actually done, and remember everyone is figuring it out.
Learned helplessness
After repeated failures that felt uncontrollable, people stop trying even when control returns. Break it with small, certain wins that rebuild a sense of agency.
Motivation myths
Motivation usually follows action rather than causing it. Waiting to feel ready keeps people stuck. Start embarrassingly small and let momentum do the rest.
Ego depletion and decision fatigue
Willpower and decision quality tend to drop when tired, hungry, or after many decisions. Make important choices earlier in the day and automate small ones.
Status games
Much human behavior is quiet competition for status: clothes, cars, opinions, even humility. Noticing the game lets you choose which ones are worth playing.
Reading a room
Watch for energy, who defers to whom, what topics make people tense, and what gets laughs. Adjust volume and humor to the room; the same joke can kill or bomb depending on the audience.
